name: Black pepper
what: The dried berries of Piper nigrum, a vine native to the Western Ghats of south India. For two thousand years it was the most traded spice in the world.
why: Pepper pulled Rome's gold to India, made Venice and then Lisbon and Amsterdam rich, and sent the first Portuguese and Dutch fleets into the Indian Ocean.
now: Vietnam grows about a third of the world's pepper; India, Brazil and Indonesia follow.

sources.cite: Turner, J. (2004). Spice: The History of a Temptation. HarperCollins.
Keay, J. (2006). The Spice Route: A History. University of California Press.

stops.note: Black pepper grows wild in the monsoon forests of the Western Ghats; the Malabar coast of Kerala is its home and was its only big source for over a thousand years.
Peppercorns were packed into the nostrils of Ramesses II when he was mummified in 1213 BCE, the oldest pepper ever found outside India. How it reached Egypt is unknown.

Once Rome took Egypt (30 BCE), ships rode the monsoon straight across the Arabian Sea to Muziris. At the Red Sea port of Berenike archaeologists found 7.5 kg of black peppercorns in a large Indian jar in a temple courtyard.
stops.meet: a ship's crewman at Berenike, or a trader at Muziris

stops.note: Camel trains crossed the desert to Coptos on the Nile, and boats took the cargo down to Alexandria. A second-century papyrus, the Muziris papyrus, records one ship's cargo worth enough to buy an estate.
Domitian built the Horrea Piperataria, warehouses for pepper and spices, by the Forum around 92. Pliny complained that India drained the empire of 50 million sesterces a year.
Besieging Rome in 408, Alaric the Goth demanded 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver and 3,000 pounds of pepper to go away.
stops.meet: a Roman during Alaric's first siege

stops.note: Marco Polo claimed Hangzhou ate 43 cartloads of pepper a day, and that for every shipload going to Christendom a hundred went to Zaiton (Quanzhou). His numbers are boasts; the scale of China's demand was real.
Venetian state galleys bought pepper at Alexandria and Beirut and sold it across Europe; for two centuries Venice set Europe's price.
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498. Asked what he had come for, his men are said to have answered: Christians and spices.
stops.meet: a trader in Calicut when da Gama's ships arrived

stops.note: Planted in northern Sumatra by about the 13th century, probably carried by Indian traders; Sumatra and Java became the second great pepper coast.
Da Gama's surviving ships brought pepper home round the Cape in 1499, worth many times the cost of the voyage. Lisbon's Casa da Índia became the king's spice house.
Portugal sold its pepper wholesale through its factory at Antwerp, which grew into Europe's richest trading city.
The first Dutch fleet, under Cornelis de Houtman, reached Banten, the pepper port of west Java, in 1596. Six years later the Dutch East India Company was founded.
De Houtman's ships came home in 1597 with a small cargo of pepper but enough profit to set off a rush of Dutch voyages east.

Captain Jonathan Carnes brought a cargo of Sumatran pepper home to Salem in 1797; for forty years Salem ships dominated the west Sumatra pepper coast, and Salem's motto still reads "to the farthest port of the rich East".
Grown in southern Vietnam since at least the 1600s, pepper boomed in the Central Highlands after the 1990s. Vietnam became the world's largest producer and exporter around 2001.
